title: How much is it?
goal: Counting to a million, bargaining at the market, and paying — while seeing why Mongolian numbers have two faces.
bekal: say and understand numbers up to a million in tugrik
ask prices, ask for a lower one, and count your change
use the *-н* form of numbers before nouns without thinking

dialogs.title: Яриа — Захад
dialogs.intro: Budi goes to Naran Tuul Market with Sarnai to buy wool socks and a scarf.

lines.speaker: Худалдагч:
lines.literal: good is Q! what take Q?

lines.speaker: Худалдагч:
lines.id: Yes, very good wool. Camel wool.
lines.literal: there-is, very good wool. camel's wool.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: That's expensive. Can you lower it a bit?
lines.literal: price-with thing is. cheap-ish make-ing may Q?

lines.speaker: Худалдагч:
lines.id: Take two pairs. That makes twenty-five thousand.
lines.literal: two pair take. twenty five thousand becomes.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: If two pairs are twenty thousand, we'll take them.
lines.literal: two pair twenty thousand if let's-take.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: OK, deal. How much is that scarf?
lines.literal: OK, let's-deal. that scarf how-much Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: If we take both, what's the total?

lines.speaker: Худалдагч:
lines.id: Sixty thousand. I've already given you a discount.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: OK, thank you. Here's a hundred thousand.

lines.speaker: Худалдагч:
lines.id: Your change is forty thousand. Come again!

notes: ⚠️ **Хэд asks for an amount; хэдэн asks "how many" before a noun.** *Үнэ хэд вэ?* (How much is it?) but *Хэдэн ном вэ?* (How many books?). The difference is like "how much is it" versus "how many books".

**Мянга = thousand, and Mongolians almost always give prices in thousands without naming the currency.** *Арван таван мянга* = 15,000 tugrik. Adding *төгрөг* isn't wrong, but it sounds like filling in a form.
**За is the word you'll hear most all day in Mongolia.** It means "good", "OK", "fine then", "well", and also fills pauses like "um". If you could take only one word from this unit, take *за*.

**Bargaining at the market is not just allowed but expected** — at the *зах* (open market) and small shops. ⚠️ In supermarkets, modern stores, and restaurants, nobody bargains, and trying will make things awkward. The line is the same as in most countries where haggling is normal.

**The suffix -хан / -хон turns an adjective into "rather" or "fairly".** *Хямд* (cheap) → *хямдхан* (fairly cheap); *ойр* (near) → *ойрхон*. This suffix softens a request — just like "a little" in "could you take a little off?"

grammars.title: Numbers have two faces
body: This is the only complication in Mongolian numbers, and once you see the pattern, it's done in five minutes. Numbers standing alone use one form; numbers **before a noun** use another form ending in **-н**.
after: **The pattern is one sentence: add -н, and if the base ends in a consonant, slip in a vowel so it can be pronounced.** *Гурав* → *гурван*; *ес* → *есөн*; *хорь* → *хорин*. Only *нэг* and *хоёр* don't change at all.

⚠️ The *-н* form is the one used for **prices, ages, times, dates, and any quantity** — because they all stand before a noun. The bare form is used only when you count aloud or answer "how many" with a single word.

grammars.title: Building big numbers
body: Mongolian builds numbers much like English: from largest to smallest, with no linking word at all. No "and" (as in British "a hundred and five"), and no reversal like German.
after: ⚠️ Note the tens, each with its own shape, which you must learn: 30 *гуч*, 40 *дөч*, 50 *тавь*, 60 *жар*, 70 *дал*, 80 *ная*, 90 *ер*. Before another number, all of them take *-н*: *гучин*, *дөчин*, *тавин*, *жаран*, *далан*, *наян*, *ерэн*.

**Mongolia's currency is the төгрөг (TÖG-rög), written ₮.** One tugrik is worth very little, so everyday prices run from thousands to tens of thousands. A bottle of water is about 1,500₮, a bowl of soup 8,000₮, a bus fare 500₮.

rows: Can you make it a bit cheaper?

blocks.title: ⚠️ Болох уу — the magic phrase that opens every door
items: *болох уу?* literally means "may it become?" and works like "may I …?" / "can I …?" in English.
Pair it with the *-ж / -ч* form of any verb: *үзэж болох уу?* (may I look?), *орж болох уу?* (may I come in?), *суух болох уу?* (may I sit?).
The answer is *Болно* (yes, you may) or *Болохгүй* (no, you may not).
This one pattern replaces ten polite sentences. Learn it today.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Цагаан* (white) is one of the most culturally loaded words in Mongolian. White means pure, good, and holy: *цагаан сар* is the Mongolian New Year ("white month"), *цагаан идээ* means all dairy foods, and *цагаан сэтгэл* means "a clean heart". If you call something *цагаан*, you are praising it.

Notice too that *хөх* means blue **and** bluish green — the line between blue and green in Mongolian isn't drawn exactly where English draws it. The sky is *хөх тэнгэр*, and that eternal blue sky is both a national symbol and the root of Mongolian belief before Buddhism arrived.

These counting words — *аяга* (cup), *ширхэг* (piece, item), *хуудас* (sheet), *хос* (pair) — work just like "cup of", "sheet of", and "pair of" in English. **You already know the idea**; you only need the vocabulary. The difference: Mongolian also uses *ширхэг* for things English counts directly, like eggs.

blocks.title: Phone numbers and years
items: Phone numbers are read **digit by digit**, using the bare form: *есөн есөн, гурав хоёр, нэг найм…*
Years are read as a whole number: 2026 = *хоёр мянга хорин зургаан он*. ⚠️ Don't split it into "twenty twenty-six" as in English.
*он* = year (in dates); *жил* = year (length of time). *2026 **он*** but *гурван **жил*** (three years long).
Dates: *арван таваны өдөр* or more often just *арван тавны*, "the fifteenth".
Can you make it a bit cheaper?
